sections.title: How topics are chosen.
sections.text: A topic gets a statement only if the parties' former MKs actually differ on it in the Knesset record: at least {min_lists} evaluated lists with {min_mks} or more former MKs on the topic, a spread of their positions of at least {min_spread}, and at least {min_names} distinct bills (a re-submitted bill counts once) sponsored by them. The thresholds were chosen in October 2026 by testing which values gave positions that held between the 24th and 25th Knesset, and were frozen on 18 October 2026; the same thresholds apply to every topic, and the full history of the choices is in the project's decision log (open source). Topics where all lists did the same, or where too few bills exist, are left out — even when they are important. When one topic lies almost entirely inside another, a shared bill counts toward only one of them, chosen by whether voters would see two different questions.

sections.title: Important topics that are not in the quiz, and why

bullets.lead: The lists' records hardly differ — nearly everyone pushed the same way:
bullets.text: relief for war and terror victims; support for families with children; credit and mortgages (credit for households falls just below the spread threshold); tax enforcement; support for charities; banning harmful online and broadcast content.

bullets.lead: Too few lists have a record once budget votes are set aside:
bullets.text: the power of labor unions; defamation law; assisted reproduction.

bullets.lead: Too few bills by the candidates to place the lists:
bullets.text: abortion; who is registered as a Jew; the Law of Return for grandchildren of Jews; gun licensing; immunity for soldiers; laws tied to a state of emergency; the Yemenite children affair; the autonomy of minors; cameras in kindergartens and institutions; the term of Supreme Court justices; sports on free channels.

selecting judges (in «Politicians' influence over the courts»); the weight of the Attorney General (in «Ministers' control over senior officials»); civil marriage and divorce (in «Civil marriage» and «Divorce»); conditions on funding religious schools (in «Funding schools without the core curriculum»); alternatives to military service (in «Drafting yeshiva students»); international law and UNRWA (in «Foreign states and international organizations in Israel»); the death penalty and sanctions on terrorists' families (in «Counter-terrorism measures»); judicial review of government decisions (in «Overriding court rulings»); preferences for underrepresented groups (in «Benefits for those who served»); surveillance powers of the security services (in «Protection of personal data»); bank fees and duties (in «Protecting the weaker party to a contract»); local preference in government purchasing (the mirror of «Imports and competition»).

bullets.lead: Bills on unrelated subjects, no single honest question:
bullets.text: bans on publishing victims' details; state ownership of disputed property; co-owners' rights in apartment buildings; accountability of individual officials; criminal liability of officials for abuse of office.

bullets.lead: Administrative matters with no position a voter would hold:
bullets.text: licensing procedures for businesses and professions; terms and deadlines; the size of public bodies; inheritance law; state awards.

sections.after: Not present at all, because no bill of a former MK carries the topic in a way that separates the lists: the Gaza war and the hostages, a Palestinian state, the cost of living as such. The quiz measures legislation, not campaigns.

sections.title: Where a list's position comes from.
sections.text: Only from what its candidates who were MKs in the 24th–25th Knesset did: the bills they sponsored, their votes on private bills, their votes on the other camp's bills and, for coalition parties, their votes on the government's own bills. A government bill counts for both camps the same way; votes on the omnibus budget laws count for nobody, because a vote for or against the whole budget says nothing about its hundred separate articles. Promises and speeches are not used. Sponsoring a bill counts {vote_ratio} times more than a vote on it: the record of a party that pushed for a change is louder than the record of a party that only voted against it — a deliberate choice, stated here so that it can be judged.

sections.title: Whose record a list carries.
sections.text: A list's record is the record of its candidates who were MKs — for a joint list that can be mostly the former MKs of one partner. The results carry a note when few former MKs stand behind a list. A former MK who moved to another list counts for the list they run with in 2026: it is the same person and their own votes.

sections.title: Leaders with few bills of their own.
sections.text: Ministers and prime ministers rarely sponsor bills, so a list's position rests mostly on its other former MKs and on votes.

sections.title: Lists with one former MK
sections.text: are shown but not ranked: one person's record is too thin to call a list the closest.

sections.title: The order of questions.
sections.text: The first {core} statements are the same for everyone: markers of the main axes along which the lists differ. The next {clarify} are chosen one at a time to tell apart the lists closest to you so far; a list that fell behind early is not probed further. Which statements are asked also depends on a rating, made by a language model, of how much a typical voter cares about each topic; it affects only which questions you see, never the closeness.

sections.title: The answer scale.
sections.text: Closeness compares directions, not intensity: if you answer «strongly agree» to everything, the result is the same as «agree» to everything; the strength of an answer matters when your answers are mixed. If you answer at random, lists without a close neighbour (the Arab lists, for example) come first more often than others — the result means something only for considered answers.

sections.title: «No clear position».
sections.text: A list is marked so when its position is weaker than {close} — below that, the side of the same list did not hold between the two Knessets in most cases — or when it rests on a single former MK or a single bill.

sections.title: Notes.
sections.text: “Few former MKs: N” — the list's position rests on very few people. “Position known for only N% of your answers” — the list has a position on less than half of what you answered, so it is shown below the others and not ranked. Lists without any former MKs have no record in the Knesset and cannot be compared.

sections.title: Limitations — what this quiz can and cannot tell you.
sections.text: The quiz is an orientation, not a precise measurement. We state openly where the data and the analysis are noisy:

bullets.lead: Only the Knesset record of former MKs
bullets.text: (24th–25th Knesset) is used. New candidates, platforms and statements are not seen. {evaluable} of {lists} lists can be evaluated; {single} {single?list|lists} with a single former MK {single?is|are} shown but not ranked; {no_record} {no_record?list has|lists have} no record.

About 98 % of votes follow the voter's bloc. A party's votes on the other camp's laws, and a coalition party's votes on the government's laws, are partly party discipline, not only conviction; that is why a vote weighs a quarter of a sponsored bill.

bullets.lead: Leaders and ministers sponsor few bills,
bullets.text: so a list's position rests mostly on its other former MKs and on votes.

bullets.lead: Topic labels were made by a language model
bullets.text: and corrected by other models: on a blind sample checked against an independent labeling, the topic was right in about 81 % of cases (89 % counting the secondary topic) and the side in about 93 %. The systematic checks that followed removed 1 607 labels, added 632 and changed 52 signs — each change only where two independent checks agreed; a further 26 522 double counts between nested topics were removed. Individual mistakes remain.

bullets.lead: Checks so far were done by models, not by people.
bullets.text: Agreement figures measure consistency between models, not accuracy for real voters; no list's position has yet been confirmed by a person who knows the Knesset.

Lists with close values cannot be told apart reliably, so values are shown rounded and should be read as «about as close». «No clear position» means the record is weak or rests on a single former MK or a single bill.
(«even if …») is not measured: the record shows what a list's bills and votes pushed for, not whether it accepts that price.

bullets.lead: A vote against a bill can mean the opposite of what the topic sign says
bullets.text: — a party may vote against a draft law because it is too lenient, not because it opposes the draft. The method cannot see the reason for a vote.

statements.agreeCountsDown: Agreeing with the statement counts as down.
